newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Paris rates stable but autumn rise doubtful.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Paris rates stable but autumn rise doubtful.

text.p: Ex-Paris cargo rates were stable as North American carriers expressed mixed feelings on the lack of impact of the strong dollar saying autumn increases must now be considered doubtful, a Reuters survey showed.
American Airlines (AA) has been the only carrier to increase its French franc rates over the six weeks with rises working out at an average of six percent to U.S. destinations, effective June 2.
AA operates daily passenger services from Paris to New York, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Dallas.
The absence of the normal impact of the strong dollar on the ex-Paris air cargo market is under discussion among transatlantic carriers.

"We are in a worrying situation. Despite the dollar going from strength to strength and industrial activity in the U.S. picking up over several months now - making French goods less expensive for the country's importers - there just hasn't been the surge of demand one would have expected and which we saw in spectacular fashion in the late 1980s when the dollar was also strong. This begs the question whether the U.S. is finding an alternative line of supply to France with south-east Asia being a probable source of origin," a TWA cargo official told Reuters.
However, American Airlines was more upbeat on the impact of the strong dollar.

"Our ex-Paris volumes have benefited from the climate of economic confidence in the U.S which has led to firms increasing their inventories and the strengthening dollar has played its part," a Paris-based AA cargo official said.

"It's been a good first half to the year and we are still filling flights pretty well even though the "holiday dip" appears to have come earlier than last year when demand was sustained until the end of July. Who knows, it may turn out to be a stronger August than last year.'
"Overall, the market is buoyant and there is no reason to believe that the final quarter of the year will be anything but strong," the official added.
Another U.S. carrier, United Airlines, also pointed to sustained demand as the market approached its summer lull which normally runs between July 15 and September 15.

This week, UAL launched a daily service Boeing 777 passenger service between Paris and San Francisco effectively doubling cargo capacity on the route which was previously operated by 767-300s, a UAL cargo official said.
While carriers may differ on the impact of the strong dollar, there is general agreement it has eaten into dollar revenues.

"Our revenues are earned in francs but remitted in dollars which has given rise to a shortfall because of the exchange rate. This could be compensated by rates increases in the autumn but try telling that to forwarders!," a Paris-based cargo spokesman for one airline said.
For the majority of carriers on transatlantic routes it is a little too early to broach the question of autumn rises.

"Frankly, we are more preoccupied with the low level of rates for spot shipments as a result of abundant capacity from Paris, normal market behaviour at this time of the year, to speculate what might happen in the autumn," a Continental Airlines cargo official said.

A TWA cargo official said: "It'll be difficult to get rate increases through in the autumn simply because of the amount of capacity which is likely to be on offer. Passenger activity has recovered and airlines might be tempted to prolong part of their summer schedules into the winter season which would be bad news for rates increases. At best, we will be able to maintain rates at current levels."

UAL was also sceptical of higher rates but for different reasons: "No one is going to begin considering rates increases in the autumn until after the summer lull but already the prospect is a slim one simply because the system of two rises a year (April and October) has become less and less credible. Customers would much prefer to negotiate at the end of the year for rates which would take effect from the new year," the UAL official added.
One forwarder did venture to suggest that if there was going to be rates increases in the autumn, then North America was probably the most likely sector for rates increases.

"This could happen on selected routes in this sector, largely because, overall, rates are at a very low level and one will probably find the airlines presenting a united front to push through raises," Alain Meister managing director of Tous Transport Aerienes (TTA), one of France's air forwarding agents, said.

Herbert de St Simon, chairman of TTA's sister company, SCAC Air, said: "The U.S west coast, notably Los Angeles must be a candidate for increases given that currently it is only one franc/kilo above the going rate for New York despite being served by considerably fewer frequencies from Paris."

In the Latin America sector, TTA's Meister said there was a prospect of a dip in rates. "The conditions are there for such an eventuality - elevated rates and expanding capacity. More and more carriers will target this region as ripe for an aggressive policy on prices."

However, Jean-Claude Junin, air cargo manager of LEP France, discounted this. "In the Spring, Varig increased rates and cargo capacity on the Paris-Sao Paulo route. One can't really see these decisions being undermined during what is likely to be a strong final quarter to the year."
